ai.title: Centralize PostHog analytics event strings into shared constants
ai.summary: AnalyticsEvent enum in common/src/constants/analytics-events.ts centralizes PostHog event names. Web components replace hardcoded strings with enum references. Scope covers authentication, cookie consent, onboarding, install dialogs, home page, demo terminal, and UI elements. Ensures consistent event naming and reduces drift across web surfaces.

eli5.text: If you interact with the website today, whether you accept or decline cookies, sign in, finish onboarding, copy an install command from the home page or install dialog, click a "Learn More" feature link, or type into the demo terminal, the analytics events that track those actions now use a single shared list of names instead of each spot making up its own label. That means the same action will always be recorded under the same event name across the site, so the team sees consistent data with less chance of typos or drift. For you, nothing in the product looks or behaves differently; this is behind-the-scenes housekeeping that makes the tracking names reliable without changing anything you can see or do.

ai.title: Refactor onboarding flow to support dynamic steps and referral codes
ai.summary: Onboarding logic shifts to dynamic step counts based on referral code presence, replacing static constants. Referral pages now render directly via OnboardClientWrapper instead of a dedicated client component. Scope covers web/src/app/onboard, web/src/app/referrals, and shared onboarding components. Progress state initializes to step 1 and persists packageManager selection.

eli5.text: The onboarding wizard now shows a different number of steps depending on whether you arrived with a referral code, and referral landing pages reuse the same step flow instead of a separate page. If you click a referral link, you'll see the welcome card and then proceed through the standard setup steps with the referral code already filled in, rather than being sent to a dedicated referral-only screen. This is live today for anyone signing up through a referral link or visiting the referrals area.

ai.title: Remove unused ANTHROPICAPIKEY2 and OPENAIKEY
ai.summary: Removes unused ANTHROPIC_API_KEY2 and OPEN_AI_KEY from env schema and .env.example. Adds CLAUDE_CODE_KEY mapping to ANTHROPIC_API_KEY in ClaudeRunner constructor for evals. Deletes unused backend/src/llm-apis/openai-api.ts type definition.

eli5.text: The team cleaned up leftover API keys from the configuration files, removing two keys that were no longer being used by the system. If you were setting up your local development environment using the example file, you would now use a single key called CLAUDE_CODE_KEY instead of separate keys for Anthropic and OpenAI. The internal tool that runs automated tests now correctly maps this new key to the system it needs. Since these were inactive keys, most people will not notice any difference in their day-to-day work.

ai.title: Remove unused GEMINI, DEEPSEEK, HELICONE env keys
ai.summary: GEMINI_API_KEY, DEEPSEEK_API_KEY, HELICONE_API_KEY removed from .env.example and packages/internal/src/env.ts schema. Unused keys cleaned up. Covers backend env validation. Removes z.string().min(1) constraints and process.env mappings.

eli5.text: The assistant has stopped reading three specific secret keys named Gemini, DeepSeek, and Helicone from its configuration files, leaving only the keys it actually uses. If you manage these settings, the assistant will no longer look for those three entries in your environment variables. Nothing breaks for users, the assistant simply ignores them now.

ai.title: Use runId for programmatic step sandbox
ai.summary: Switched programmatic step caching and QuickJS sandbox keys from `agentId` to `runId` in `run-programmatic-step.ts` and `quickjs-sandbox.ts`. Added `runId` to `AgentState` type in `agent-definition.ts`. Prevents state leakage when agents reuse IDs across different runs.

eli5.text: Each time you run an agent, the system now uses that specific run's unique ID to manage temporary workspaces where the agent's code executes and caches its progress. Previously, it keyed off the agent's ID, which meant if two separate runs shared the same agent ID, they could accidentally share or overwrite each other's cached state and code sandbox, leading to data leakage. You would not see anything on your screen, but if you reuse the same agent across multiple runs, this prevents one run from peeking into or corrupting another's stored data.
